newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai baht pressure eases now, but threat remains.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht pressure eases now, but threat remains.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand's move to rule out devaluation might have staved off attacks on the weak baht temporarily, but risks still remain, analysts said on Tuesday.

If the economic data over the next three months showed no improvement in exports growth and the wide current account deficit, the central bank could find its back against the wall amid depleting reserves to defend the currency, they said.

The baht has been under attack since late last year. The dollar/baht midrate, fixed daily by the central bank, is currently 25.99 baht, the lowest since May 4, 1990,and down from 25.56 on December 3 and 25.71 on January 20.

However, the consensus among analysts was that the central bank would not resort to devaluation as a way out as it would do more harm than good to the Thai economy. And if the devaluation came, it would very likely to be forced from the outside.

"The Bank of Thailand needs time. Time for expected improvement in key economic indicators to show through and time for recent policy measures to work their way through the economy," SBC Warburg said in a new report.

"Our view is that the BoT has successfully staved off the current round of speculative pressure on the Thai baht...To appreciate the BoT's position, remember that a forced devaluation will only exacerbate strains in the system," it said.
The central bank on Thursday issued a statement reiterating its firm stance that baht devaluation was definitely not a policy option to tackle Thailand's current economic problems.

The current account deficit is estimated at 8.2 percent of GDP for 1996 although with a recent massive cut in spending, the gap this year is expected to narrow to 7.4 percent from 7.7 forecast earlier.
Exports are expected to have contracted 0.1 percent in 1996 compared with growth of 23.6 percent in 1995. The Bank of Thailand has forecast that exports will grow 7.7 percent in 1997.

The sliding export growth, the level of the current account deficit and doubt over the soundness of the financial sector due to the level of loans to a depressed property sector, prompted foreign investors and speculators to bail out of the baht on a belief that a Mexico-style devaluation was inevitable, dealers said.
Goldman Sachs in a report last week said there was a chance of a 25 percent devaluation of the baht.
Speculative attacks by offshore operators that followed the report forced the Bank of Thailand to use its robust reserves to defend the currency.

The baht is fixed daily against the dollar at a midrate based on a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar which caused the currency to slide as the dollar spiralled. Its steep fall against the dollar aggravated the speculative selling.
Market sources estimated that the central bank used between $3-10 billion to defend the currency since December.
Although some observers expressed scepticism over the Bank of Thailand's statement, they agreed that the move to some extent restored confidence inthe baht.
"I don't agree with the Bank of Thailand that the baht is not overvalued. Actually, I think the baht should stand around 27 to the dollar at current a value," said one Hong Kong-based fund manager.
"Nevertheless, their strong statement restores confidence as it indicated that the country will be serious in solving the economic problems to make devaluation out of question," he said.
Standard Chartered said Thailand was facing hard times but cyclical economic recovery was on the way and devaluation should not be an option.

"Ongoing negativity and nervousness continue to plague the market. We feel the risks have increased but we find overly negative sentiment is overshadowing the marginally improving fundamentals," the bank said in its research.

"However, over the ensuing months, the authorities will have to act with prudence, austerity and timeliness. Therefore, we see the baht remaining stable, and the BoT not changing its foreign exchange policy soon," it said. -- Bangkok newsroom (662) 652-0642
